title: Slices and maps
summary: The two data structures you use constantly, and the aliasing that surprises everyone.

concepts.title: What a slice actually is
concepts.brief:
A slice is **not** an array. It is a small three-field value — a pointer to an array, a **length**, and a **capacity** — and it is copied by value like any other struct.

- `len(s)` — how many elements you can index right now
- `cap(s)` — how many fit before the backing array must be replaced

Slicing never copies the data. `b := a[1:3]` makes a new header pointing into `a`'s array. Both now share the same memory, which is the source of nearly every slice surprise.

examples.label: Three fields, one array
examples.code:
a := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
b := a[1:3]

len(b)  // 2   - elements 20, 30
cap(b)  // 4   - from index 1 to the end of a's array

b[0] = 99
fmt.Println(a)  // [10 99 30 40 50]  <- a changed
examples.note: `cap` of a re-slice runs to the end of the backing array, not to the end of the slice you cut from.

examples.label: Making one on purpose
examples.code:
s := make([]int, 0, 100)   // len 0, cap 100
s = append(s, 1)           // no allocation, cap was already there

t := make([]int, 5)        // len 5, cap 5 - five zeroes, already addressable
t[0] = 1                   // fine

var u []int                // nil: len 0, cap 0
u = append(u, 1)           // fine - append allocates
examples.note: `make([]int, 5)` and `make([]int, 0, 5)` are very different: the first has five usable zeroes, the second has none.

choices: [10 99 30 40 50] — b points into a's array
[10 20 30 40 50] — slicing copies the elements
It panics; b has length 2 and cannot be written to
items.explain: Slicing is a view, not a copy. `b[0]` is `a[1]`. If you need independence you must copy explicitly: `b := make([]int, 2); copy(b, a[1:3])`. This is the mechanism behind "I passed a slice to a function and it modified my data" — the header was copied, the array was not.

items.prompt: `a` has length 5. What are `len` and `cap` of `a[1:3]`?
choices: len 2, cap 4 — capacity runs to the end of the backing array
len 2, cap 2 — capacity matches the new length
len 3, cap 5 — the bounds are inclusive
len 2, cap 5 — capacity is always the original array's size
items.explain: len 2, cap 4: from index 1 to the end of the array. That extra capacity is what lets a later `append` to this slice overwrite `a[3]` instead of allocating. The three-index form `a[1:3:3]` caps it at 2 and makes the next append allocate — the standard way to hand out a slice safely.

items.prompt: `s := make([]int, 5)`. What does `s[0] = 1` do, and what does `len(s)` return?
choices: Works; len is 5 — the slice already holds five zeroes
Panics; len is 0 — the second argument is capacity
Works; len is 0 and becomes 1 after the assignment
Does not compile; make needs three arguments for slices
items.explain: `make([]int, 5)` is length 5 — five usable zeroes. The two-argument form sets length; the three-argument form `make([]int, 0, 5)` sets length and capacity. Mixing them up gives you either a panic on index, or a slice with five unwanted zeroes in front of your appended data.

items.prompt: `var s []int` — a nil slice. Which of these work without panicking?
choices: `len(s)`
`s = append(s, 1)`
`for _, v := range s`
items.explain: Everything except indexing. A nil slice is a perfectly good empty slice: `len` is 0, `range` runs zero times, and `append` allocates on first use. Only indexing fails, with `index out of range [0] with length 0`. This is why idiomatic Go declares `var results []T` and appends, with no initialization.

concepts.title: append, and when it copies
concepts.brief:
`append` has two completely different behaviors and you cannot tell which you got without looking at `cap`:

- **Room left** (`len < cap`) — it writes into the existing array and returns a header with a bigger length. Anything else sharing that array **sees the change**.
- **No room** — it allocates a new, larger array, copies everything over, and returns a header pointing somewhere else. The original is now **detached**.

This is why `append`'s result must always be assigned: `s = append(s, x)`. Ignoring the return value is a bug the compiler does catch, because the result would be unused.

examples.label: Same call, two different outcomes
examples.code:
a := make([]int, 3, 4)   // [0 0 0] with room for one more
b := a[:2]               // shares the array

b = append(b, 99)        // room available -> writes a[2]
fmt.Println(a)           // [0 0 99]   <- a changed

c := make([]int, 3, 3)   // no spare room
d := c[:2]
d = append(d, 99)        // no room -> new array
fmt.Println(c)           // [0 0 0]    <- c untouched
examples.note: Identical code, opposite results, decided entirely by spare capacity. This is the bug that only shows up once the input grows.

examples.label: Appending to a shared slice in a loop
examples.note: `in[:0]` is the idiomatic zero-allocation filter. It is also a trap if anyone still holds `in`.

items.prompt: `a := make([]int, 3, 4)`, `b := a[:2]`, then `b = append(b, 99)`. What is `a`?
choices: [0 0 99] — there was spare capacity, so append wrote into a's array
[0 0 0] — append always allocates a new array
[0 0 99 0] — a grows to length 4
It panics — b cannot grow past its length
items.explain: `cap(b)` is 4 and `len(b)` is 2, so there was room and append wrote in place, clobbering `a[2]`. Had the capacity been exactly 3, append would have allocated and `a` would be untouched. Whether a shared slice gets corrupted depends on capacity you probably never checked.

items.prompt: Why must you write `s = append(s, x)` rather than just `append(s, x)`?
choices: append returns a new header; the original s may still have the old length
Purely stylistic — append also mutates s in place
Because append can panic if the result is discarded
It is required only for slices created with make
items.explain: `s` is a value holding pointer/len/cap. `append` cannot change *your* copy of that value, so it returns a new one — with a longer length, and possibly a different pointer. Discarding it loses both. Go makes this one hard to get wrong: `append(s, x)` alone is a compile error, since its result is unused.

items.prompt: Which builtin copies elements from one slice into another that already has length?
items.explain: `copy(dst, src)`. It copies `min(len(dst), len(src))` elements and returns that count — so `copy(make([]int, 0), src)` copies nothing, a classic mistake. Allocate with the right *length*, not capacity: `dst := make([]int, len(src))`.

items.prompt: Put the steps of an append that outgrows its capacity in order.
steps: append sees len == cap, so there is no room
A new, larger array is allocated
The existing elements are copied into it
The new element is written after them
A new header pointing at the new array is returned
items.explain: The copy is why appending in a loop without a capacity hint is O(n) allocations and a lot of copying. Growth is amortized — roughly doubling for small slices and tapering off — but if you know the final size, `make([]T, 0, n)` skips all of it.

concepts.title: Maps
concepts.brief:
A hash table with built-in syntax. Three things decide most of how you use it:

- The zero value is **nil**: reads work, writes panic. Always `make` it.
- Lookup always succeeds. A missing key gives you the value type's zero, which is why the **comma-ok** form exists: `v, ok := m[k]`.
- A map value is **not addressable**. You cannot take `&m[k]`, and you cannot assign to a field of a struct stored by value in a map.

Maps are also **not safe for concurrent use**. Concurrent writes produce `fatal error: concurrent map writes`, which is a runtime crash that `recover` cannot catch.

examples.label: Comma-ok, and why zero is ambiguous
examples.code:
counts := map[string]int{"a": 0}

counts["a"]        // 0 - present, value zero
counts["zzz"]      // 0 - absent

v, ok := counts["a"]     // 0, true
v, ok = counts["zzz"]    // 0, false
examples.note: Without comma-ok there is no way to tell "stored zero" from "not there". The same form works for type assertions and channel receives.

examples.label: Struct values in a map are not addressable
examples.note: Maps can rehash and move their contents, so Go refuses to hand out a pointer into one.

items.prompt: `m := map[string]int{"a": 0}`. How do you distinguish a stored zero from a missing key?
choices: `v, ok := m["a"]` — ok is false only when the key is absent
Compare against nil: `if m["a"] != nil`
Use `len(m)` before and after the lookup
You cannot; a stored zero is indistinguishable from a missing key
items.explain: The comma-ok form. A plain lookup returns the zero value for a missing key, so `if m[k] != 0` conflates "absent" with "present and zero" — a real bug in anything counting things or holding `map[string]bool`. The same two-value form works for `v, ok := x.(T)` and `v, ok := <-ch`.

items.prompt: `m` is a `map[string]P` where P is a struct. Why does `m["a"].N = 2` fail to compile?

code.label: go build
code.text: ./main.go:8:2: cannot assign to struct field m["a"].N in map

choices: Map values are not addressable — a map may move them when it rehashes
The map was declared with a value type instead of a pointer type
Struct fields can only be assigned through a method
The map key must be addressable before its value can be
items.explain: Growing a map can relocate every entry, so a pointer into it would dangle — Go refuses to create one. Two fixes: store `*P` instead of `P`, or do read-modify-write. Storing pointers is usually right when the struct is mutated often, and wrong when you wanted value semantics.

items.prompt: Two goroutines write to the same plain map at the same time. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: `fatal error: concurrent map writes` — the process dies, and recover cannot stop it
A panic that the http server recovers like any other
One write silently wins; maps are atomic per key
Nothing — the runtime locks maps internally
items.explain: `fatal error`, not `panic`. The runtime has a cheap detector for this and it kills the process immediately — `recover` does not apply to fatal errors. Guard the map with a `sync.Mutex`, or use `sync.Map` for the narrow cases it suits. `go test -race` finds this long before production.

items.prompt: `var m map[string]int` — a nil map. Which of these are safe?
choices: `len(m)`
`delete(m, "x")`
items.explain: Everything but the write. `delete` on a nil map is explicitly a no-op, and reads return zero with `ok` false. Only assignment panics. So a nil map is a usable read-only empty map — handy for optional config, dangerous the moment something writes to it.

items.prompt: Write the expression that creates an empty, writable `map[string]int` using the builtin.
items.explain: `make(map[string]int)`, or the literal `map[string]int{}` — both give a real, writable map. `make` takes an optional size hint, `make(map[string]int, 1000)`, which pre-allocates buckets and avoids rehashing when you know roughly how many keys are coming.

concepts.title: range, and what it gives you
concepts.brief:
`range` hands you a **copy** of each element. Assigning to the loop variable changes nothing in the collection — to mutate, index into it: `s[i].Field = x`.

Map iteration order is **deliberately randomized**. The runtime starts at a random bucket on every run, specifically so nobody can write code that depends on an order that was never guaranteed. If you need a stable order, collect the keys and sort them.

What `range` yields depends on the type: index+value for slices and arrays, key+value for maps, byte-offset+rune for strings, and a single value for channels.

examples.label: The loop variable is a copy
examples.note: This is the slice equivalent of the value-receiver mistake, and just as silent.

examples.label: Sorted iteration over a map
examples.note: The single-variable form `for k := range m` gives keys only. For a slice, `for i := range s` gives indexes only.

code.label: main.go

choices: [{false} {false}] — `it` is a copy of each element
[{true} {true}] — range yields references into the slice
It does not compile; `it` is not addressable
[{true} {false}] — only the first iteration takes effect
items.explain: `range` copies each element into the loop variable, so the writes land on throwaway copies. Use the index: `for i := range items { items[i].Done = true }`. The copy also costs real time for big structs — ranging over `[]BigStruct` copies every one of them.

items.prompt: You range over the same unmodified map twice in one program run. Is the order the same?
choices: Not guaranteed — the runtime randomizes the starting point each time
Yes, within a single run it is stable; only across runs does it change
Yes, maps iterate in key insertion order
Yes, maps iterate in sorted key order
items.explain: Randomized per iteration, on purpose. Early Go had incidentally-stable ordering, people depended on it, and their code broke when the implementation changed — so the team made it visibly random. To get deterministic output, extract the keys and `sort` them.

items.prompt: Match what `for a, b := range x` yields for each type of x.
pairs: index and a copy of the element
key and value, in random order
received values only — one variable, not two
items.explain: The string case catches people: the index is a **byte** offset, so it jumps by more than one across multi-byte characters. The channel case has no second variable at all, and the loop ends when the channel is closed.

items.prompt: `for _, v := range items { go func() { use(v) }() }`. In Go 1.22 and later, what does each goroutine see?
choices: Its own value — loop variables became per-iteration in Go 1.22
The last element, because all closures share one variable
A random element, depending on scheduling
A compile error; closures cannot capture loop variables
items.explain: Per-iteration since Go 1.22. Before that, every closure captured the one shared `v` and usually saw the final element — the single most reported Go gotcha ever, which is why it was changed. The old workaround `v := v` is now redundant but harmless. The behavior follows the `go` directive in `go.mod`, so an old module keeps the old semantics.
